hints: Focus on the definition of disproportionation, where the same element in one starting species is both oxidised and reduced to two different products.
Check the oxidation number of bromine in reaction 1, it starts at 0 in $\text{Br}_2$ and goes to -1 in $\text{Br}^-$ and +1 in $\text{OBr}^-$.
Now work out bromine in reaction 2 from +1 in $\text{OBr}^-$ to -1 in $\text{Br}^-$ and +5 in $\text{BrO}_3^-$, then see if both reactions fit the definition.
walkthrough:
**Recall what disproportionation means**

A disproportionation is when the same element in the same reactant is both oxidised (oxidation number increases) and reduced (oxidation number decreases). We just need to track bromine.

Rule to use:
$$\text{oxidation number increase = oxidised, oxidation number decrease = reduced}$$

**Analyse reaction 1**

In $\text{Br}_2$, each Br is 0. In products, Br in $\text{NaBr}$ is -1, and Br in $\text{NaOBr}$ is +1.

Check $\text{OBr}^-$: $\text{O}$ is -2, overall -1, so $\text{Br}$ is +1:
$$0 \rightarrow -1 \text{ (reduction) and } 0 \rightarrow +1 \text{ (oxidation)}$$ 
So the same $\text{Br}_2$ is both oxidised and reduced. Reaction 1 is a disproportionation.

**Analyse reaction 2**

Here the reactant bromine is all in $\text{OBr}^-$, so Br starts at +1. In products, Br in $\text{Br}^-$ is -1, and Br in $\text{BrO}_3^-$ is +5.

Check $\text{BrO}_3^-$: $3 \times (-2) + \text{Br} = -1$, so $\text{Br} = +5$:
$$+1 \rightarrow -1 \text{ (reduction) and } +1 \rightarrow +5 \text{ (oxidation)}$$ 
So again the same starting bromine is both oxidised and reduced. Reaction 2 is also a disproportionation.

**Conclude**

Since both reaction 1 and reaction 2 show bromine being simultaneously oxidised and reduced, both are disproportionations.

options.A: Correct. Reaction 1 changes Br(0) to Br(-1) and Br(+1). Reaction 2 changes Br(+1) to Br(-1) and Br(+5). Both meet the definition of disproportionation.
options.B: Incorrect. This would mean no oxidation number splitting occurs, but bromine clearly changes to both higher and lower states in both reactions.
options.C: Incorrect. Reaction 1 is correctly spotted, but reaction 2 is missed. Students often miss it because the reactant is a compound ($\text{NaOBr}$) not an element, yet Br(+1) still splits to Br(-1) and Br(+5).
options.D: Incorrect. Reaction 2 is correctly spotted, but reaction 1 is missed. Students sometimes think NaOH must be involved in redox, but Na and O and H do not change, only Br(0) splits to -1 and +1.
